questions.stem: What is being investigated in this practical?

options.text: The effect of different solids on the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide
options.explanation: The aim names both the varied factor, the solids, and the reaction, peroxide breakdown.

options.text: The effect of temperature on dissolving
options.explanation: No dissolving or heating belongs to this aim.

options.text: The effect of acid concentration on marble chips
options.explanation: That is the surface area practical.

options.text: The amount of oxygen in air
options.explanation: That is the rusting practical from an earlier topic.

questions.stem: Which gas is collected in the measuring cylinder?

options.text: Oxygen, released as the hydrogen peroxide decomposes
options.explanation: Peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen, and the oxygen is collected.

options.text: Hydrogen, from the breakdown of water
options.explanation: Water is the other product and stays liquid.

options.text: Carbon dioxide from the air
options.explanation: Air is not part of the reaction.

options.text: Steam from the catalyst
options.explanation: The catalyst stays solid and cool.

questions.stem: Why is the gas volume read after a fixed time for every catalyst?

options.text: A shared time window makes the volume readings comparable between solids
options.explanation: Equal windows turn gas volume into a fair ranking of speeds.

options.text: Because the cylinder empties itself after that time
options.explanation: Nothing empties automatically.

options.text: Because the peroxide runs out exactly then
options.explanation: Peroxide supply is not the reason for the shared window.

options.text: Because catalysts stop working after that time
options.explanation: Catalysts keep working; the window is for comparison.

questions.stem: Manganese(IV) oxide gives the largest gas reading of the four solids. What does that show?

options.text: It is the most effective catalyst of those tested for this decomposition
options.explanation: Most gas in the shared window means the fastest catalysis.

options.text: It must have been the heaviest powder
options.explanation: Mass is not the comparison; catalytic effect is.

options.text: It made the peroxide more concentrated
options.explanation: Concentration of peroxide is fixed across runs.

options.text: It proved the other solids were not catalysts at all
options.explanation: The others may still catalyse, just more slowly.

questions.stem: Which feature of the method shows that the solids act as catalysts rather than reactants?

options.text: Each solid can be recovered unchanged after speeding up the same reaction
options.explanation: Unchanged recovery is the signature of catalysis rather than consumption.

options.text: The solids dissolve completely in the peroxide
options.explanation: Dissolving would suggest reaction, not catalysis.

options.text: The solids change colour permanently
options.explanation: Permanent change would point to reaction.

options.text: Each solid appears in the product formula
options.explanation: Catalysts never enter the product side.

questions.stem: State the piece of apparatus that connects the conical flask to the inverted measuring cylinder in the peroxide practical.
questions.modelAnswer: A delivery tube carries the oxygen gas from the flask to the inverted measuring cylinder.

questions.stem: Name the four solid candidates that can be tested on hydrogen peroxide in this investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: The candidates are manganese(IV) oxide, lead(II) oxide, iron(III) oxide and copper(II) oxide.

questions.stem: Explain why the bung must be closed before the catalyst is added in the gas-volume experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: Closing the bung first stops oxygen escaping, so all the gas made flows along the delivery tube into the measuring cylinder and the volume recorded in the fixed time is the true amount.

questions.stem: A student tests copper(II) oxide and then repeats the run with iron(III) oxide. State the purpose of repeating the run with each solid.
questions.modelAnswer: Repeating the experiment with different catalysts lets their gas volumes in the fixed time be compared, so the fastest candidate can be ranked fairly.

questions.stem: Why plot all catalysts on the same graph rather than four separate ones?

options.text: A shared graph makes the relative rates immediately comparable
options.explanation: One shared axis turns separate readings into a ranking.

options.text: Because separate graphs are not allowed in chemistry
options.explanation: No such rule exists; the reason is comparability.

options.text: To save paper
options.explanation: Convenience is not the analytical reason.

options.text: Because each catalyst changes the time window
options.explanation: The window is fixed for all, which is why one graph works.

questions.stem: A catalyst reading equals the with-no-catalyst run. What is the fairest conclusion?

options.text: That solid is not acting as an effective catalyst for this decomposition
options.explanation: Matching the baseline means no catalytic effect was observed.

options.text: The solid must be a reactant
options.explanation: No effect is not evidence of reaction.

options.text: The gas was collected wrongly
options.explanation: Apparatus worked for every other run.

options.text: The peroxide had already decomposed completely
options.explanation: Other readings show peroxide was still active.

questions.stem: Which condition makes the plotted comparison fair?

options.text: Every bar shares the same fixed time window and the same peroxide supply
options.explanation: Identical conditions mean only the catalyst differs.

options.text: Each catalyst received a different amount of time
options.explanation: Different windows would bias the heights.

options.text: The graph uses different units per bar
options.explanation: Mixed units would destroy comparability.

options.text: Only the best catalyst was plotted
options.explanation: The ranking needs all candidates.

questions.stem: What does the spread of bar heights across the four oxides demonstrate?

options.text: Different solids catalyse the same reaction at different rates
options.explanation: Height spread maps directly onto catalytic effectiveness.

options.text: The peroxide concentration varied between runs
options.explanation: Concentration was controlled, not varied.

options.text: Catalysts work only at high temperatures
options.explanation: Nothing in this practical involves heating.

options.text: The oxides are consumed at different speeds
options.explanation: Catalysts are not consumed at all.

questions.stem: How could the investigation be extended after the graph is drawn?

options.text: Test additional solids with the same fixed-time method and add them to the graph
options.explanation: The method extends naturally to more candidates under identical conditions.

options.text: Change the time window for each new solid
options.explanation: Changing windows would break comparability.

options.text: Replace the peroxide with a different solution and keep the bars
options.explanation: Swapping the reaction invalidates the shared graph.

options.text: Abandon measurement and rank by powder colour
options.explanation: Colour carries no rate information.

questions.stem: State why all the catalyst results are plotted on one graph.
questions.modelAnswer: All the results share one graph so the speeds of the different catalysts can be ranked against each other.

questions.stem: On the shared graph, which reading identifies the fastest catalytic decomposition tested?
questions.modelAnswer: The tallest reading on the graph marks the fastest catalytic decomposition tested.

questions.stem: Explain why every reading must share the same time window for the comparison to be fair.
questions.modelAnswer: Each gas volume is measured over the same fixed time, so the readings differ only because of the catalysts; different windows would give longer runs an unfair advantage.

questions.stem: One candidate solid gives a negligible gas reading on the shared graph. State what this shows about the solid.
questions.modelAnswer: A negligible reading shows the solid is acting as a poor catalyst for the decomposition, barely speeding the reaction up at all.
